paragraphs.heading: Where plates meet
paragraphs.text: Earth's lithosphere is the planet's rigid outer shell, made up of the crust and the upper mantle. It is broken into seven or eight major plates, the count depending on the definition used, plus many minor plates. A plate boundary is the place where two plates meet. How the two plates move relative to each other decides the type of boundary: convergent, divergent or transform.

paragraphs.heading: Why plates can move
paragraphs.text: Earth's outer layers are split into two: the lithosphere and the asthenosphere. The lithosphere is the cooler and more rigid of the two. The asthenosphere is hotter and flows more easily. The lithosphere exists as separate tectonic plates that ride on the asthenosphere. Being relatively rigid, the plates float across the ductile asthenosphere below.

paragraphs.heading: Where the action is
paragraphs.text: Plate boundaries are where geological events happen. Earthquakes occur there, and surface features are created there, such as volcanoes, mountains, oceanic trenches and mid-ocean ridges. Of the world's active volcanoes, the vast majority lie along plate boundaries. The Pacific plate's Ring of Fire is the most active and widely known. Some volcanoes do occur in the interiors of plates.

paragraphs.heading: Convergent boundaries
paragraphs.text: Along a convergent boundary, a process called subduction takes the edge of one plate down beneath the other and into the mantle. This reduces the total surface area of Earth. At a subduction zone, oceanic crust that is relatively cold and dense sinks into the mantle. That sinking limb is the strongest driver of plate motion.

paragraphs.heading: Divergent margins
paragraphs.text: Along divergent margins, new oceanic crust forms by seafloor spreading. This new crust balances the surface lost to subduction, which keeps the total surface area constant, like a tectonic conveyor belt. At a seafloor spreading ridge, which is a topographic high, the plates travel away from the ridge. Newly formed crust cools while moving away, and that makes it denser and adds to the motion.

paragraphs.heading: Thin at ridges, thick at trenches
paragraphs.text: Oceanic lithosphere forms at mid-ocean ridges and spreads outward, so its thickness depends on how far it is from the ridge where it formed. As time passes it cools, and the mantle next to it below is cooled too and added to its base. For a typical distance travelled before being subducted, it goes from about 6 km thick at mid-ocean ridges to more than 100 km at subduction zones.

paragraphs.heading: How fast
paragraphs.text: Plates typically move relative to each other at somewhere between zero and 10 cm a year. At the Mid-Atlantic Ridge the motion is 10 to 40 millimetres per year, about as fast as fingernails grow. The Nazca plate moves at about 160 millimetres per year, about as fast as hair grows.
